title: Introduce a concept named threads to better describe concurrency
body:
We have various "in parallel" algorithms that actually need to do message passing with some sort of background thread in order to provide some guarantees. E.g., doing `new SharedWorker()` in two separate processes should not cause two fetches to happen and they should not race for creating a global environment either. Instead, they should both run an action on a background thread. Whoever gets to run their action first does not matter much (that can race), but the actions cannot run at the same time.

Having this kind of concept would basically be formalizing "in parallel". While discussing with @jyasskin we identified a couple of interesting things:
- Some threads need a name (e.g., "shared worker manager")
- Threads should probably have the same lifetime as the user agent so we don't have to worry much about starting and stopping it
- Threads need to be able to hold onto some state (a "shared worker manager" needs to know about any allocated workers)
- Communication is through some kind of message passing. I'm not sure how much we want to formalize that at the start.
- Message passing needs to be possible between threads, and between threads and event loops
- We should perhaps formalize the concept of a "system call". These can all be synchronous.
- Having a convenient shorthand to start a thread, run some action in that thread and then once that completes run some action in the thread/event loop that started the whole thing might be nice. Basically some kind of promise-wrapper. A lot of fetch usage is like this.

This is a new thing and would basically help us to be better explain the various concurrent aspects of the web platform. It'll likely need various iterations and some usage by a couple of features before we settle on the right shape.

Also paging @dherman as he once mentioned that the "in parallel" idea lacked some conceptual backing.
